metadata.description: A Process Resource Entity (resource-service-entities §6) — an automation job as a first-class node in the dependency graph: playbook, workflow, pipeline, or script. Its depends_on edges are PROCESS dependencies and carry the same weight as infrastructure dependencies: while the job is running, nothing it depends on may be taken down. This is what makes orchestrated lifecycle operations (a UPS-triggered graceful shutdown, a rolling upgrade) derivable from true data — the orchestrator host, the switch fabric the job traverses, and the name service it resolves through are the job's real dependencies, so 'orchestrator stops last' and 'connectivity outlives compute' fall out of the reverse-topological sort with no policy special-casing. Vendor engines are providers, never the type. First registry type with entity_type Process; §6.4 obliges entities modified by this job to cite its uuid in their provenance.

context.purpose: Makes an automation job (playbook, pipeline, script) a first-class node in the dependency graph — carrying the job's own portable intent (definition_ref, parameters, targets, schedule) — so what the job needs stays up while it runs and the job itself survives an engine change. outputs-exempt: run-scoped — every run-history fact (state, timestamps, counts, the change-set a run produced, its evidence artifact) is an output of a RUN INSTANCE, not of the job: runs instantiate the process (Process-family model) and carry their own records. Job-level copies would project instance facts onto the definition — the compute-never-store rule forbids storing them, and the definition/instance separation forbids homing them here even as derivations. The run instance type (Process family, P1) declares these outputs; bindings that need them bind there.
context.plain_description: A record of a job that automation runs — a playbook, a CI pipeline, a backup script. It is modeled like infrastructure because it has real dependencies: the host it executes on, the network fabric it traverses, the name service it resolves through. While the job runs, none of those may be taken down, which is how ordered operations like a UPS-triggered graceful shutdown come out of the data instead of hand-written runbooks. The record also carries the automation intent itself: which definition the job executes (definition_ref), the parameters it is invoked with, the resources it operates on (targets), and — for scheduled jobs — when it runs and how overlapping or missed runs are handled (schedule). Because that intent lives on the record and not inside any engine, moving the job to a different engine is a provider change on an untouched definition. Each run publishes typed outputs — terminal state, timestamp, run count, a change-set, and an evidence reference — so two engines running the same job are comparable by diffing declared outputs. The engine that runs the job is a provider detail, not part of the type.
use_when: You need a shutdown or upgrade sequence to know an orchestration job is running and must finish before its executor host stops.
You need to record which automation created or modified a resource, so the resource's provenance can cite the job.
You need a scheduled or event-triggered job (cron, a UPS on-battery event) tracked with a hard execution-time limit.
You need the job's automation intent — definition, parameters, targets, schedule — recorded portably so an engine migration is a provider swap that leaves the intent and the job's identity untouched.
You need to verify a new engine (or an engine upgrade) against the incumbent by re-running an idempotent job and requiring an empty change-set in the typed outputs.
not_for: The long-running service a job might deploy — that is Software.Service; a service has no scheduled end, a job must declare max_execution_time.
The workload container a job runs in — that is Compute.Container; the job is the process, not the runtime.
works_with: Compute.BareMetalHost — the executor host a running job pins (the orchestrator stops last).
Network.Switch — the fabric the job traverses; connectivity outlives whatever the job operates on.
Network.AddressService — the name resolution the job needs to reach its targets.

process_type.description: Process class (resource-service-entities §6.3). 'other' is the escape hatch — the enum stays closed.

max_execution_time.description: ISO 8601 duration (e.g. PT30M). MANDATORY per ENT-004; enforced by the substrate Lifecycle Constraint Enforcer.

on_max_exceeded.description: Action when max_execution_time is exceeded. Default is profile-governed (ENT-004).

trigger.description: What initiates the job (e.g. a NUT on-battery event, a cron schedule, an operator).

definition_ref.description: The versioned definition artifact this job executes — the playbook, workflow, pipeline, or script the engine runs. Always a typed reference, never an inline body or a provider-native id: either a resource Reference (common-elements §2.5) to the entity carrying the definition, or a data_reference (ADR-012) pinning an immutable automation_definition reference-data layer version — the pin that lets each promotion stage run exactly the definition version it verified, and lets rehydration replay the intent together with its payload. Optional: a job discovered on a brownfield engine may not yet cite its definition.

parameters.description: Parameters the definition is invoked with — the org-authored automation intent (a patch policy, a reboot policy, maintenance windows) that must survive an engine migration byte-identical. Keys are defined by the referenced definition; the substrate carries them opaquely and the provider validates them against the pinned definition at naturalization (T9 — the substrate never translates them into a provider-native spec).

targets.description: The resources this job operates on — typed resource References (common-elements §2.5), never inventory strings. Each entry is authored by target_handle (ADR-025 §2 — a uuid is never hand-authored; DCM resolves and pins target_uuid at reserve). Part of the portable automation intent: the target set is engine-neutral and unchanged by an engine migration. Distinct from the informational affected_entities edge: targets is authored intent (what the job is FOR); affected_entities records what a run actually touched.

schedule.description: Scheduled-execution intent — meaningful only when trigger is 'schedule'. Carries the data the trigger enum value alone cannot: when the job runs, what happens when a run would overlap a still-running predecessor, and what happens to a missed window.

expression.description: Schedule expression, cron syntax (adopted vocabulary: Kubernetes CronJob .spec.schedule). The provider naturalizes it to its native scheduler.

overlap_policy.description: What happens when a scheduled run fires while the previous run is still executing (CronJob concurrencyPolicy cross-walk): allow concurrent runs, forbid the new run, or replace (supersede) the running one.

missed_run_policy.description: What happens to a run whose window was missed (engine down, job suspended): skip it, or catch_up — run once as soon as possible (CronJob startingDeadlineSeconds semantics).

relationships.name: executor_host
relationships.description: Executor host(s) — where the job runs. A running job pins its executor: in a reverse-topological lifecycle operation the executor cannot stop until the job completes ('orchestrator stops last', derived, not special-cased).

relationships.name: fabric
relationships.description: Fabric the job traverses to reach its targets — connectivity outlives whatever the job is operating on.

relationships.name: resolver
relationships.description: Name/address resolution the job uses to reach targets (typically soft — inventories can pin IPs).

affected_entities (§6.3) — entities this job creates/modifies/decommissions. Informational; §6.4 makes the provenance obligation flow the OTHER way (affected entity cites the job uuid). NOTE: the declared target is representative — affected entities may be of ANY resource type; this edge is informational and never constrains what a job may touch (the former bare 'Compute' category target was not a registered type).

adopts.role: run-to-completion and scheduled-job vocabulary (activeDeadlineSeconds ≈ max_execution_time, terminal states; CronJob schedule/concurrencyPolicy/startingDeadlineSeconds ≈ schedule.expression/overlap_policy/missed_run_policy)
